title: Me and White Supremacy: Combat Racism, Change the World, and Become a Good Ancestor
author: Layla F. Saad
target_audience: White readers seeking to understand privilege and systemic racism
Educators and facilitators of diversity and inclusion discussions
Organizations and book clubs addressing racism and equity
core_themes: Identifying and unpacking internalized white supremacy
Understanding privilege, fragility, and complicity in racist systems
Taking accountability for personal and collective behaviors
Promoting lifelong antiracist action and allyship
Legacy and responsibility to future generations
primary_purpose: To guide readers—particularly those who hold white privilege—through a process of honest self-examination and personal accountability regarding white supremacy, with the goal of inspiring committed, ongoing antiracist action.

structure_format.organization: 28-day structured workbook, with daily topics, prompts, and exercises

key_concepts_lessons: White supremacy is not just overt acts of racism but also a system upheld by beliefs, actions, and inactions.
Privilege can be invisible to those who hold it, and recognizing it requires discomfort and honesty.
Accountability and self-reflection are crucial steps toward becoming an effective antiracist.
White fragility, tone policing, color blindness, and performative allyship are barriers to true progress.
Antiracism is an ongoing, lifelong process, not a one-time achievement.
Personal transformation is linked to collective liberation and justice.
notable_features: Structured as a 28-day challenge with daily exercises
Focus on journaling as a tool for self-discovery and accountability
Originally developed as an Instagram challenge and workbook, refined into a published book
Interactive format that requires reader participation
Emphasis on collective responsibility and legacy
cultural_historical_context: Emerged during a period of heightened reckoning with racial injustice, particularly following the Black Lives Matter movement resurgence in the late 2010s and early 2020s. The book's origin from social media reflects changing methods of engagement with social justice topics.
reception_impact: Became a New York Times bestseller and major antiracism resource in 2020 and beyond
Widely adopted in workplaces, book clubs, and educational settings
Praised for its directness, practical structure, and effectiveness as a transformative tool
Sparked dialogue and self-examination among white readers, but also faced resistance from some for its demand for personal accountability
Cited as an entry point into deeper antiracist learning and action
comparable_titles: So You Want to Talk About Race by Ijeoma Oluo
How to Be an Antiracist by Ibram X. Kendi
Between the World and Me by Ta-Nehisi Coates
